title: A trailing blank line in a CSV file parses as a real (empty) row, and indexing into it throws
assumption: A CSV file's trailing newline (or a blank line left at the end by whatever produced it) just gets dropped, so the number of parsed rows always equals the number of visible data lines.

input.display:
a,b
1,2

 (note the extra blank line before end of file)
input.description: A CSV generated by exporting from a spreadsheet or database tool that leaves one truly empty line at the end of the file, as opposed to a single ordinary trailing newline after the last data row (which is harmless).

what_goes_wrong:
A single trailing line ending after the last row (`a,b
1,2
3,4
`) parses cleanly as three rows - but an extra blank line (`a,b
1,2

`) parses as three rows in Python where the last one is a genuinely empty list `[]`, so `rows[-1][0]` raises `IndexError: list index out of range`. The JS naive `split("
")` equivalent doesn't crash on this particular shape, but produces two phantom `[""]` rows.
why: A CSV reader has to distinguish "the file ends after a newline" (no extra row) from "there is a genuinely empty line in the data" (a zero-field row). Python's `csv` module does the former correctly and represents the latter faithfully as `[]`, which is correct behavior but a shape callers rarely expect to handle, so indexing into the last row without checking its length crashes. Plain `text.split("\n")` in JavaScript produces a trailing empty string element whenever the text ends in a newline at all, so naive code gets an extra `[""]`-shaped phantom row even for the harmless single-trailing-newline case that Python's real parser handles cleanly.

repros.code:
import csv, io
clean = 'a,b\r\n1,2\r\n3,4\r\n'
print(list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(clean))))
with_blank = 'a,b\n1,2\n\n'
rows = list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(with_blank)))
print(rows)
try:
    print(rows[-1][0])
except IndexError as e:
    print("IndexError:", e)

fix: Filter out zero-length rows (Python: `if row` after reading) or trailing empty lines before splitting (JS), and never index into the last parsed row without checking it has the expected number of fields first.

sources.title: Python docs: csv - CSV File Reading and Writing
RFC 4180: Common Format and MIME Type for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) Files

test_cases.note: A CSV-parsing function given a file with a genuinely blank trailing line should represent it as an empty row (as Python's csv.reader does) rather than crashing - callers must then check row length before indexing.
A single CRLF after the last row is just the line terminator: exactly two rows, no phantom empty row and no stray \r in the last field.
